findings.detail: The paper lists the cumulative total across savings programmes from 2008 to 2027, described as £767m per annum.
findings.matters: A cumulative savings record of this length is a benchmark for other councils assessing how much more savings they can realistically deliver.
findings.figures: £767m cumulative savings from annual budget since 2008
findings.quote: £767m from our annual budget since 2008

findings.paper_title: HCC budget-consultation-27-28-information-pack
findings.headline: Hampshire's two current savings programmes are planned to deliver £152m by 2028/29, with £134m to be delivered by 31 March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper says the savings have already meant reducing some services, and that further savings could mean more reductions.
findings.matters: A finance officer can compare the planned delivery profile of these programmes with their own savings timetable.
findings.figures: £152m planned by 2028/29; £134m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: £134m will be delivered by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: HCC budget-consultation-27-28-information-pack
findings.headline: Hampshire says it can no longer deliver sufficient savings to bridge its budget gap.
findings.detail: The paper attributes this to the level of savings achieved to date and the scale of the challenge ahead. It says reserves have been used to balance the budget since 2022/23 and are now running out.
findings.matters: A council stating that savings alone can no longer close its gap is a signal a lender or peer would weigh against its own savings pipeline.
findings.figures: £198.9million budget gap for 2027/28
findings.quote: we can no longer deliver sufficient savings to bridge our budget gap.

findings.paper_title: HCC budget-consultation-27-28-information-pack
findings.headline: Hampshire forecasts a 2027/28 budget shortfall of £198.9million, described in the paper as the highest gap it has ever faced.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast gap assumes council tax rises by 4.99%. It describes the shortfall as the difference between the cost of services and the funding available.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this gap against their own forecast and the scale of the options needed to close it.
findings.figures: £198.9million budget gap for 2027/28; 4.99% assumed council tax rise
findings.quote: the highest gap we have ever faced.

findings.paper_title: Budget management - month 4 - Report No. FIN2617
findings.headline: Two council commercial properties have business tenants at risk of administration, creating income and debt recovery risk
findings.detail: The council notes that two properties in its commercial portfolio have business tenants currently at risk of entering administration. This creates unquantified risk to the rental income streams that support council operations, and potential for uncollectable debts.
findings.matters: Property rental income is material to council finances; tenant insolvencies can create both income loss and additional costs (rates, maintenance) on vacant properties.
findings.figures: Two properties identified; financial impact not quantified
findings.quote: There are currently two properties within the council's portfolio with leases to businesses considered to be at risk of administration. Therefore, there are risks to future income at these sites and a potential that outstanding debts will be uncollectable.

findings.paper_title: Budget management - month 4 - Report No. FIN2617
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs forecast to rise £700k in 2027/28 after grant condition change
findings.detail: After the February budget was set, the council's homelessness grant conditions were changed to exclude temporary accommodation support. This creates an identified cost pressure of approximately £700k for 2027/28 MTFS, representing a structural budget challenge that will need to be addressed in next year.
findings.matters: Identifies a material structural cost pressure emerging for 2027/28; shows how external policy changes can significantly impact council budgets.
findings.figures: £700k cost pressure identified in 2027/28 MTFS
findings.quote: Change in homelessness grant conditions now excludes temporary accommodation. Next year there is a increased cost of circa £700 k in the MTFS reported to 4th August Cabinet.

findings.paper_title: Budget management - month 4 - Report No. FIN2617
findings.headline: Interest and MRP savings of £1.2m from property disposals and early £2.1m loan repayment
findings.detail: The council has achieved interest savings of £758k and MRP savings of £427k, largely from disposal of 168 High Street (£2m), Optrex Lane (£1.5m), and early repayment of a £2.1m loan by Farnborough International. These are one-off items that contribute to the headline underspend but do not reflect structural budget improvement.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council's ability to generate cash through asset sales and early debt repayment, though one-off nature means benefits do not repeat in future years.
findings.figures: £758k interest saving; £427k MRP saving; £2.1m loan early repayment; £2m and £1.5m property disposals
findings.quote: Early repayment of £2.1m loan by Farnborough International

findings.paper_title: Budget management - month 4 - Report No. FIN2617
findings.headline: Union Yard capital receipt forecast down £1.3m from original plan; other major disposals delayed 16-18 months
findings.detail: The council's largest planned capital receipt, Union Yard (82 units), has fallen from original forecast of £15m to current forecast of £13.676m, a shortfall of £1.324m. Devereux House and Hawley Lane are delayed 18 and 16 months respectively. These shortfalls and delays increase the council's borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: Capital receipts fund investment programmes; shortfalls materially increase borrowing needs and affect medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Union Yard: original £15m (Sep-25), forecast £13.676m (Jul-26), shortfall £1.324m, delay 10 months. Devereux House delayed 18 months. Hawley Lane delayed 16 months.
findings.quote: Union Yard - 82 units ... Latest Forecast Value 13,676 ... Total Change in Value (1,324) ... Total Delay in months 10

findings.paper_title: Budget management - month 4 - Report No. FIN2617
findings.headline: Council forecasts £1.2m revenue underspend despite identified February 2026 financial sustainability challenge
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget for 2026/27 after identifying a significant financial sustainability challenge in February 2026. At month 4 (end of July), the forecast projects an overall revenue underspend of £1.2m, composed of £426k service underspends, £758k interest savings, and £427k MRP savings largely from property disposals.
findings.matters: Shows whether a council managing identified financial pressures can maintain budget position; the underspend suggests the position is being held, though largely from one-off items rather than structural improvements.
findings.figures: £1.2m total underspend; £426k service level; £758k interest savings; £427k MRP savings
findings.quote: The latest forecast shows savings of £1.2m are anticipated for the 2026/27 outturn position.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Service savings strategy abandoned; discovered significant savings could not be achieved without adversely affecting service delivery
findings.detail: The 2025/26 MTFS required recurring service reductions of £1.78m, increasing to £3.781m by 2027/28. A discovery phase concluded that 'significant savings or lower-priority services could not be readily identified without adversely affecting service delivery.' The council then ceased this savings strategy, switched to relying on reserves, and moved planned efficiencies to the North Hampshire Unitary Authority.
findings.matters: The council has abandoned sustainable cost-cutting and is instead treating short-term reserve depletion as its financial strategy, suggesting structural problems with its cost base.
findings.figures: 2025/26 required service reductions: £1.78m. Planned 2027/28 reduction: £3.781m (no longer pursued).
findings.quote: it ceased the service prioritisation savings strategy, maintained a no net budget growth approach other than unavoidable pressures, and planned to use reserves where necessary.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Council reserves will be drawn down to fund structural deficits, with estimated £2.253m available at Vesting Day before risks
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £2.362m deficit in 2025/26 (now better at £2.362m from reserves). Going forward, it plans deficits of £442k in 2026/27 and £2.694m annually from 2027/28, to be met from reserves. Estimated available reserves at Vesting Day: £2.253m, but this is before accounting for the risks outlined (property income, receipts delays, Serco, LGR).
findings.matters: The council is structurally deficit and treating reserves as a funding source, not a contingency, with limited buffer remaining against the material risks identified.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn deficit: £2.362m. Reserves at 31 March 2026: £6.914m. Estimated at Vesting Day: £2.253m (before risks).
findings.quote: the estimated revenue reserves available to fund the forecast deficit at Vesting Day have increased from £1.828 million to £2.253 million before consideration of the risks outlined below.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs expected to be significant but not yet budgeted in the MTFS
findings.detail: LGR cost apportionment methodology across Hampshire is still being assessed. Costs are expected to be significant and will place 'additional demands on available reserves.' While some may be funded through Flexible Use of Capital Receipts, 'a substantial proportion is expected to fall directly on the revenue budget.' No additional provision has been included in this MTFS update beyond existing assumptions.
findings.matters: A material unfunded cost burden is likely to emerge after this MTFS was set, putting further pressure on reserves and cashflow.
findings.figures: None quantified in the paper; costs still being assessed.
findings.quote: These costs are expected to be significant and will place additional demands on available reserves. While some expenditure may qualify for funding through the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Direction, a substantial proportion is expected to fall directly on the revenue budget. No additional provision has been included within this MTFS update beyond existing assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Serco contract renegotiation concluding September 2026 with risk of cost pressures beyond current £1.095m budget
findings.detail: Contract negotiations conclude in September 2026. The council has provisioned £500k plus a further £595k in the current forecast. Under either the existing arrangement or a move to Twin Stream model, the council must procure and fund vehicles and equipment. The paper acknowledges 'risk of additional cost pressures arising beyond the current budget assumptions.'
findings.matters: A major service contract is being renegotiated with material uncertain costs that could exceed budget in either outcome scenario.
findings.figures: February 2026 provision: £500k. Additional assumed in current review: £595k. Total: £1.095m.
findings.quote: The Council will be able to either continue the existing contract arrangements or move to a Twin Stream service model. Under either option, the Council will be responsible for procuring and funding vehicles and equipment. There remains a risk of additional cost pressures arising beyond the current budget assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Audit of 2025/26 outturn not yet completed; adjustments could materially impact reported position and forecasts
findings.detail: The 2025/26 position reported in this paper is provisional. The council explicitly notes it 'has not yet achieved an unqualified audited financial position' and that audit adjustments could impact the reported outturn and forward financial forecasts. Any such impacts will be reflected in subsequent monitoring reports.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on the financial position stated here—the final audited outturn and any audit qualifications could reveal material issues not currently disclosed.
findings.figures: Reported 2025/26 outturn deficit: £2.362m (provisional, unaudited).
findings.quote: Given that the Council has not yet achieved an unqualified audited financial position, there remains a risk that adjustments arising from the completion of the audit process could impact the Council's reported financial position and future financial forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Four major capital disposals all delayed 9-15 months, forcing extended external borrowing
findings.detail: Devereux House (15 months late), Hawley Lane (12+ months), Meads Block 3 (9+ months), and Union Yard (9 months, with £500k value reduction). The council explicitly states these delays 'increase the level and duration of external borrowing required to maintain liquidity.' Borrowing rates are also higher than the 4.5% assumption in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Delayed asset sales force extended external borrowing at higher rates than budgeted, materially worsening cashflow and increasing interest costs.
findings.figures: Union Yard: budgeted £15m May-25, forecast £14.5m July-26 (£500k reduction, 9-month delay). Devereux House: 15-month delay. Hawley Lane: 12+ months. Meads Block 3: 9+ months.
findings.quote: Delays in achieving planned capital receipts continue to impact the Council's treasury position by increasing the level and duration of external borrowing required to maintain liquidity. Uncertainty over the timing of asset disposals reduces flexibility in cashflow management and limits opportunities to reduce borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Commercial property income faces material decline and lease-break risk over the MTFS period
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a comprehensive review of rental income forecasts and lease expiries. Income declines from £9.8m in 2026/27 to £6.5m by 2029/30. Income at risk outside lease breaks grows from £137k to £3.2m over the period. Service costs and business rates at Ashbourne House are expected to increase significantly. The paper explicitly warns this could have 'material adverse impact on the revenue budget and the Council's financial resilience.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a major income stream is contracting and vulnerable to further deterioration through tenant defaults or lease exits.
findings.figures: Income up to lease break/exit: £9.8m (26/27) declining to £6.5m (29/30). Income at risk outside lease: £136,634 (26/27) to £3,223,907 (29/30).
findings.quote: Any reduction in occupancy levels or rental income could have a material adverse impact on the revenue budget and the Council's financial resilience leading up to Vesting Day.

findings.paper_title: FIN2616 - Treasury Management Q1 report
findings.headline: Treasury investments shifted entirely from local authority deposits (32% bail-in exposure) to pooled funds (100% bail-in exposure) in Q1 2026
findings.detail: In Q1, the council moved all short-term treasury investments from local authority deposits (bail-in exposure 32%) to money market and pooled funds with 100% bail-in exposure. The £13m in local authority deposits was entirely liquidated and reinvested elsewhere. While the shift to higher-yielding pooled funds supports income targets, it increases credit risk on what remains a small treasury investment base.
findings.matters: This represents a change in the risk profile of the council's liquidity reserves. A 100% bail-in exposure means all remaining short-term deposits could theoretically be frozen in a credit event, leaving no safe haven for emergency liquidity.
findings.figures: Total investments £23.4m; bail-in exposure increased from 32% (31 March 2026) to 100% (30 June 2026); local authority deposits fell from £13m to £0m
findings.quote: 31.03.2026: Bail-in Exposure 32%; 30.06.2026: Bail-in Exposure 100%

findings.paper_title: FIN2616 - Treasury Management Q1 report
findings.headline: Non-treasury investment income declining: forecast to fall from £8.9m to £7.6m over three years
findings.detail: The council's income from commercial and service investments (primarily the £132m property portfolio) is forecast to decline from £8.9m actual in 2025/26 to £7.9m in 2026/27 and £7.6m in 2027/28. This represents a material revenue stream that is forecast to shrink by 15%, compounded by the strategic uncertainty around the property portfolio's future.
findings.matters: For a council with net revenue stream around £17-18m, this £1.3m decline in investment income is material and suggests either deteriorating asset performance or planned disposals. A lender needs to know whether this is temporary market impact or structural decline.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual £8.9m → 2026/27 forecast £7.9m → 2027/28 forecast £7.6m
findings.quote: The Council also held £138.8m of such investments in: directly owned property £132m; loans to local businesses and landlords £4.5m; subsidiaries £2.3m

findings.paper_title: FIN2616 - Treasury Management Q1 report
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs rising: weighted average rate on maturing loans increased 32 basis points in Q1
findings.detail: The council's average rate on short-term loans rose from 4.58% three months prior to 4.90% at 30 June. With £92m of borrowing maturing within the next 24 months (25% in next 12 months, 47% in 12-24 months), refinancing at rising rates will increase revenue financing costs. The council is actively extending maturities to manage this risk, but the Q1 rate rise reflects tighter market conditions.
findings.matters: Higher refinancing costs directly increase the revenue budget pressure and reduce financial headroom. This is material when combined with £92m due for refinance in the next two years at potentially higher rates.
findings.figures: Short-term average rate 4.90% vs 4.58% prior quarter; £92m due within 24 months; total borrowing £127m
findings.quote: The average rate on the Council's short-term loans at 30th June 2026 4.90%, this compares with 4.58% 3 months ago.

findings.paper_title: FIN2616 - Treasury Management Q1 report
findings.headline: £132m commercial property portfolio now restricted from new debt financing and requires exit strategy review
findings.detail: Rushmoor holds £132m in commercial property investments purchased before CIPFA code changes that prohibited borrowing for yield-focused assets. The council is now required to review options for exiting these holdings before undertaking further additional borrowing. This represents a material strategic constraint on financial flexibility and funding capacity, with no clear timeline or market conditions for potential exits.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this £132m portfolio (127% of current net borrowing) constrains the council's ability to finance future capital investment or debt service, and whether forced asset sales could impact council finances if executed in poor market conditions.
findings.figures: £132m; net borrowing at 30 June £103.6m; external borrowing £127m
findings.quote: The Council currently holds £132m in commercial property investments of which the majority were primarily for financial return and were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: Investment income as a proportion of revenue stream is volatile and unreliable
findings.detail: Total net income from service and commercial investments as a proportion of net revenue stream jumped from 56.99% (2024/25) to 67.27% (2025/26) and is forecast to drop to 44.08% (2026/27). This large swing indicates the income is not stable and dependent on capital value or yield volatility outside the council's direct control.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the council is relying on volatile investment returns to balance the budget. The 23-point swing in one year suggests this income source cannot be reliably forecast or depended upon to sustain revenue.
findings.quote: Total net income from service and commercial investments as a proportion of its net revenue stream has been and is expected to be as indicated below. [Table showing] Proportion of net revenue stream 56.99% [2024/25] 67.27% [2025/26] 44.08% [2026/27 forecast]

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: Capital expenditure fell from £14.3m (2024/25 actual) to £5.6m (2025/26) with forecast decline to £2.7m (2027/28)
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure fell from £14.3m (2024/25) to £5.6m (2025/26) and is forecast to decline further to £3.6m (2026/27) and £2.7m (2027/28). This sharp reduction suggests either constrained borrowing capacity or policy-driven service investment reduction.
findings.matters: Lenders interpret declining capital investment as a sign of financial constraint—the council cannot afford to invest in infrastructure or may be deliberately cutting capex to preserve revenue. Either signals reduced financial headroom.
findings.quote: Capital expenditure 14.3 [2024/25 actual] 5.6 [2025/26 actual] 3.6 [2026/27 budget] 2.7 [2027/28 forecast]

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs spiked to 5–7% by end of year
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities, which had tracked between 4.0% and 4.5% for most of the year, jumped to 5.0–7.0% towards the end of the financial year. The average rate on short-term loans rose from 4.41% three months prior to 4.58% at end of March.
findings.matters: Rising short-term rates increase refinancing risk. If the council needs to roll over maturing debt, costs will be materially higher. This compounds the already-high financing cost ratio.
findings.figures: Short-term rates 5.0–7.0% end-of-year vs 4.0–4.5% earlier; average short-term rate 4.41% → 4.58%
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been similar to or a little above Bank of England Base Rate for most of the period, with interest rates between 4.0% and 4.5%. However, as is commonly seen, rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0% being seen.

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: £111m in commercial investments are blocking new borrowing until exited
findings.detail: The council holds £111m in directly owned property and other commercial investments purchased before the CIPFA Prudential Code changed to prohibit local authorities borrowing to invest primarily for yield. The executive explicitly states it will not borrow more until it has reviewed options for exiting these investments to reduce the revenue impact of holding them.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the council is asset-locked in illiquid holdings that drain revenue and prevent capital financing flexibility. The statement that new borrowing is contingent on exit strategy signals the council is aware of the problem but has not solved it.
findings.figures: £111m commercial investments, comprising £111m directly owned property, £4.5m loans to businesses, £2.3m subsidiaries
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £111m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments to reduce the impact of borrowing costs and risk on the revenue account.

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: Financing costs consumed 68.72% of net revenue stream in 2025/26, forecast to fall to 43.21% in 2026/27
findings.detail: Interest payable on loans and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) chargeably against revenue consumed 68.72% of the council's available revenue (net revenue stream from council tax, business rates, and general grants) in 2025/26. This forecast to fall to 43.21% in 2026/27, but the current ratio is extremely high.
findings.matters: A lender would see this as indicating the council has very little revenue available for discretionary spend, reserves, or responding to unexpected costs. At 68.72%, there is only 31% of revenue available for all services and contingency.
findings.quote: Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream ... 2025/26 actual 7.1 ... 68.72%

findings.paper_title: FIN2615 - Treasury Management Q4 report
findings.headline: Reserve released to cover budgetary pressures, signalling cash tightness
findings.detail: The council released £1m from a reserve that had been set aside to mitigate the impact of statutory override on pooled investment funds. The release was made due to current budgetary pressures. This signals the council is drawing down buffers to manage cash rather than accumulating reserves.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a red flag for lenders—it suggests the council is under revenue pressure and lacking headroom to absorb shocks or volatility in income.
findings.figures: £1m reserve release from statutory override provision
findings.quote: Given current budgetary pressures and the extension of the override the authority decided to release £1m from this reserve.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy - Report No. PG2604
findings.headline: Council's Financial Recovery Plan explicitly depends on estate-related income and efficiency gains
findings.detail: The strategy states the Financial Recovery Plan depends on 'strengthening income resilience, reducing avoidable estate-related costs and targeting effective disposals and reinvestment.' The estate management strategy is the mechanism for delivering these. If estate goals are not met, the financial recovery plan will not deliver as modelled.
findings.matters: A lender should verify that the financial recovery assumptions are realistic and depend on achievable estate outcomes. Failure to realise disposal proceeds or income targets would impair the council's financial position.
findings.figures: none; Financial Recovery Plan dependency not quantified
findings.quote: The Council's Financial Recovery Plan depends on strengthening income resilience, reducing avoidable estate-related costs and targeting effective disposals and reinvestment. The AMS provides the structure through which these objectives are translated into estate-related decisions.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy - Report No. PG2604
findings.headline: Property team capacity constraints could delay execution of the Financial Recovery Plan
findings.detail: The implementation is contingent on reviewing and renewing property team structure, as the current team's capability and capacity are being reviewed to ensure they can deliver the strategy. Implementation also requires a newly procured outsourced asset management contract. These dependencies introduce execution risk.
findings.matters: If the property team cannot execute the strategy—particularly disposals and income generation that the Financial Recovery Plan depends on—the council's financial position could be at risk.
findings.figures: none specific; structural review and external procurement both 'subject to formal governance'
findings.quote: Development and maintenance of individual asset management plans will require adequate capability and capacity within the property service team. The current team capability and capacity is due to be reviewed to ensure it can deliver the AMS on time and to the specification set out in the AMS.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy - Report No. PG2604
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio carries disproportionately high financial risk relative to its income contribution
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies its commercial property holdings as material to income but as representing a disproportionately high financial risk. The strategy requires development of specific quarterly monitoring (income statements, balance sheet, risk log, four-year projections feeding MTFS) because of this risk profile. This signals the council views this portfolio as unstable or volatile.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that a material part of the council's income base is acknowledged as higher-risk, and may be subject to market volatility or performance deterioration.
findings.figures: represents a material element of the council's income and a disproportionately high financial risk
findings.quote: The commercial property portfolio is not a standard council activity by its commercial nature and represents a material element of the council's income and a disproportionately high financial risk to the council. This warrants the development and support for a specific suite of quarterly income and expenditure statements, balance sheet and risk log, including a four-year projection informing the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy - Report No. PG2604
findings.headline: Significant deferred maintenance liabilities across operational and community assets could create unexpected costs
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that maintenance investment has been historically constrained, and that operational and community assets—particularly ageing buildings—now carry heightened condition, compliance and lifecycle risk. The strategy recognises these represent 'significant latent dilapidations and maintenance liability'. These liabilities need to be developed and updated to inform Medium-Term Financial Strategy prioritisation.
findings.matters: Unquantified maintenance liabilities create hidden financial exposure. If assets reach compliance or safety thresholds, sudden capital demands could force urgent spending or asset disposal at disadvantageous terms.
findings.figures: described as 'significant latent dilapidations and maintenance liability' but not quantified in this strategy document
findings.quote: The operational and community assets represent a significant latent dilapidations and maintenance liability that needs to be fully developed and updated to enable prioritisation decision making within the annual review of the MTFS, to protect asset value, health, safety and legal risk, and overall value for money in line with the AMS.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy - Report No. PG2604
findings.headline: Investment income is heavily concentrated in a small number of tenants, creating revenue vulnerability
findings.detail: The council generates approximately £11m annual income from its estate, but about a quarter of this rent comes from a small number of tenants. This concentration creates both income stability risk and exposure to individual tenant covenant failure. The strategy acknowledges this by requiring monitoring of income concentration measures for investment assets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that a significant portion of the council's income strategy depends on a narrow tenant base, which could destabilize if key tenants fail or leave.
findings.figures: approximately £11m in annual income; around a quarter of rent derived from a small number of tenants
findings.quote: The council's estate generates approximately £11m in annual income, though this is heavily concentrated, with around a quarter of rent derived from a small number of tenants.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Commercial property income of £7.9m–£8.3m covers 47–57% of financing costs; portfolio acquired 2016–2021 for financial gain
findings.detail: The council holds commercial property investments acquired 2016–2021 generating net annual income of £7.9m (2024/25 actual), £8.1m (2025/26 forecast), £8.3m (2026/27 estimate). This income covers a material proportion of financing costs: 57.1% of net core revenue stream in 2024/25, declining to 47.7% by 2026/27. Property market downturns, tenant defaults, or lease expirations could materially impair this income and worsen the council's financial position.
findings.matters: Commercial income substitutes for other revenue sources. Unlike grants or tax income, it faces market and tenant covenant risk. A lender would need confidence this income is resilient to property market stress.
findings.quote: Between 2016 and 2021 in the context of central government financial support for local public services declining, the Council undertook some investment in commercial properties purely or mainly for financial gain.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Strategic cessation of new capital borrowing; capital programme contracted from £14.7m to £3.6m over two years
findings.detail: Debt-financed capital spending has fallen from £8.4m (2024/25) to £4.3m (2025/26) to £0 planned for 2026/27 onwards. The overall capital programme has contracted correspondingly from £14.7m (2024/25) to £3.6m (2026/27), £2.7m (2027/28), £2.5m (2028/29). Future capital will be financed entirely from government grants and capital receipts. This represents a sustained tightening of capital investment capacity.
findings.matters: A council with no capacity for new capital borrowing faces constraints on asset investment and service development. Sustained under-investment in assets can lead to deterioration and reduced service capacity.
findings.quote: In 202 6/27, the Council is planning capital expenditure of £ 3.6m as summarised below

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Farnborough leisure centre capital project contingent on securing guaranteed operator income and achieving annual cost-neutrality
findings.detail: The council has included a leisure centre development at Farnborough in its capital strategy but explicitly conditions it on 'securing guaranteed operator income sufficient to fund the required borrowing to bridge the gap between the cost of build and the remaining Levelling Up Funding'. The project must also be 'at least cost neutral every year'. This is a conditional commitment, not a confirmed project.
findings.matters: A capital scheme dependent on third-party operator guarantees is higher-risk than council-funded investment. If guarantees are not secured, the project does not proceed, affecting both capital investment and debt reduction plans.
findings.figures: Farnborough leisure centre; contingent on operator income guarantee; must be cost-neutral annually; leverages Levelling Up Funding
findings.quote: The Council's ambition to build a leisure centre at Farnborough is dependent upon securing guaranteed operator income sufficient to fund the required borrowing to bridge the gap between the cost of build and the remaining Levelling Up Funding allocated by government, the overall revenue impact on the Council must be at least cost neutral every year.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: £23.6m capital receipts forecast for 2026/27 to finance capital programme; timing and proceeds explicitly flagged as uncertain
findings.detail: The council plans to receive £23.6m capital receipts in 2026/27 (up from £4.8m in 2025/26) to finance capital expenditure and debt reduction, with zero new borrowing. The strategy explicitly flags 'uncertainties around the timing of asset sales and the amount that assets can be sold for', and acknowledges these 'amounts may be different or be received in different years'. Shortfalls would delay both capital investment and debt reduction.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are essential to the council's debt reduction plan and capital programme. If sales are delayed or underprice, both investment and debt management timescales will slip.
findings.figures: £4.8m capital receipts (2025/26 forecast), £23.6m (2026/27 estimate); 2026/27 capital financing: £1.5m grants, £2.1m receipts, £0 borrowing
findings.quote: There is the possibility that these amounts may be different or be received in different years.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Borrowing of £159m declared 'not considered to be affordable on a long term, sustainable basis'; £32.9m asset sales planned over four years
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, the council holds £159m borrowing at 4.7% weighted average rate. The strategy explicitly states current debt is not sustainable and plans £32.9m of asset sales (and FIL loan repayment) over four years to reduce it. However, the council acknowledges 'uncertainties around the timing of asset sales and the amount that assets can be sold for', creating material execution risk on the debt reduction trajectory.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible path to sustainable debt. This council recognises the problem and has a plan, but depends on executing substantial asset sales at uncertain prices and timescales.
findings.figures: £159.0m borrowing at 31 December 2025; £32.9m asset sales/repayment planned over four years; financing costs 50.6% of net core revenue (2024/25)
findings.quote: The current high levels of borrowing are not considered to be affordable on a long term, sustainable basis. For this reason, asset sales (and FIL loan repayment) of £32.9m over the next four years are expected to reduce borrowing to a more affordable level.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: External auditor Ernst Young raises sustained concerns about the council's progress on achieving financial sustainability and resolving its deficit; the auditor is considering whether to issue a public interest report.
findings.detail: For the second consecutive year, Ernst Young's audit report raises concerns about the council's financial sustainability. The auditor has not ruled out issuing a public interest report—an extraordinary step that overrides normal democratic controls and escalates the council's financial situation to national scrutiny. The auditor has already held a member-only briefing to flag these concerns.
findings.matters: Independent auditor concern validates the severity of the council's financial position. A potential public interest report would be a major red flag for any lender and would trigger external intervention by government or regulator.
findings.figures: Concerns raised for second consecutive year (2023/24 and 2024/25 audit reports)
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Annual Audit report was presented to the Audit and Governance committee on 28th January 2026, and being consistent with the previous year's report, raises concerns regarding the council's progress on achieving financial sustainability and resolving its deficit. EY have a duty to consider if it is appropriate to raise a public interest report, with the very grave effect of overriding the democratic control of the council.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council's Financial Statements have disclaimed audit opinions back to 2020/21, meaning the opening reserve balances are not independently verified; full audit assurance won't be achieved until February 2029.
findings.detail: The council's external auditor (Ernst Young) has not been able to sign off on the council's accounts for several years due to audit delays. This means there is no independent verification that the reserves the council claims to hold actually exist or are adequate. The council will not have a clean audit opinion until February 2029—well into the post-merger period.
findings.matters: Unaudited reserves are unverified. A council's ability to balance its budget depends on having sufficient reserves to draw upon, but if those reserves have never been independently verified, the true financial position is unknown. There is risk that reserves are lower than stated.
findings.figures: Disclaimed audit opinions back to 2020/21; full audit assurance not expected until February 2029
findings.quote: Financial Statements disclaimed audit backlog to 2020/21 carries risk around impact on available reserves. Full audit assurance will not be achieved until the 2026/27 financial statements audit is completed by audit deadline of February 2029.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council must borrow £149m by end of 2026/27 and refinance £74m of maturing debt; interest rate sensitivity is acute—a 0.5% rate rise adds £300k annually to borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Rushmoor has substantial borrowing needs to fund capital programmes. The MTFS assumes interest rates will settle at 4.5%, but treasury officers are actively managing the timing of new borrowing to lock in rates. However, the council's budget cannot absorb unexpected rate movements. The risk register quantifies this: even a modest 0.5% increase costs £300k/year—a material portion of reserves given current constraints.
findings.matters: A council's ability to manage borrowing costs determines whether reserves last long enough to reach the merger date. Interest rate risk is real and uninsurable; rate movements are outside the council's control but directly impact budget sufficiency.
findings.figures: £149m borrowing requirement by end 2026/27; £74m debt maturing in 2026/27; assumed interest rate 4.5%; 0.5% rate rise = £300k/year additional cost
findings.quote: The council as part of its previous strategy for funding prior year capital programmes will have a need to borrow £149m by the end of 2026/27 before the application of capital receipts

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The £5m-per-annum waste collection contract with Serco has not been concluded; negotiations remain open on 'significant cost and capital commitment risks'.
findings.detail: The contract renewal is unsettled despite the contract value being approximately £5m annually. The council identifies 'significant cost and capital commitment risks' that 'must be engaged with and understood as early as possible'. No clear resolution date is given, and the risk is flagged as requiring ongoing engagement.
findings.matters: Waste collection is a core statutory service. An unresolved contract with a value equivalent to significant budget pressure means the council faces potential cost escalation or service disruption mid-financial-year if negotiation breaks down.
findings.figures: ~£5m annual contract value; specific cost and capital risks identified but not quantified
findings.quote: The Waste collection contract with Serco (circa £5m) negotiations to extend the contract have not been concluded. There are some significant cost and capital commitment risks associated with this contract that must be engaged with and understood as early as possible to enable any potential mitigation to be effective.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The Farnborough Leisure Centre project will generate £806k of net annual revenue cost between 2026 and 2028, before improving after 2028—scope and cost still being finalised.
findings.detail: The council is building a new leisure centre with uncertain final cost. The 2026/27 budget includes an estimated £806k annual revenue drain (including additional borrowing interest and MRP) for the first three years, but 'work on scoping the cost of a leisure centre on the Civic Quarter site is still underway' and a proposal will not reach Cabinet until March 2026. Budget and treasury strategies will need adjustment once Cabinet decides to proceed.
findings.matters: A major capital project with not-yet-finalised scope and cost adds revenue pressure to an already-stressed budget. If final costs exceed estimates, the council will have to find additional savings or borrowing during a period when it has little flexibility.
findings.figures: £806k net annual revenue expenditure impact 2026–2028 (including borrowing interest and MRP); project scope still being scoped
findings.quote: the council is proposing to progress the Farnborough Leisure Centre with a net revenue expenditure impact in the short-term 2026-2028 of £806k, including additional borrowing interest and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP).

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council holds an unsecured £6.5m loan to Farnborough International Limited (FIL) repayable in tranches over the next three years; FIL's financial stability is flagged as a material risk.
findings.detail: The council has lent £6.482m to a private company with no apparent security or right to recover if the company fails. The council reviews FIL's trading and cashflow quarterly, but the risk is explicitly identified in the risk register as requiring 'continue engagement'—indicating ongoing concern about repayment.
findings.matters: An unsecured loan to a potentially unstable company concentrates credit risk; if FIL defaults, the council loses £6.5m from already-depleted reserves, forcing either further asset sales or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £6.482m unsecured loan due in tranches over three years
findings.quote: There is an unsecured loan to Farnborough International Limited (FIL) of £6.482m due for repayment in tranches in the next three years.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: If the council's planned merger into a new unitary authority is delayed beyond April 2028, the 2028/29 budget position will require a Section 114 notice—effectively ceasing all non-essential spending.
findings.detail: The council's financial projections assume the merger completes on schedule. The S151 officer warns that if the merger is delayed, the 2028/29 projection 'will, based upon these projections, require a S114(3)'. A Section 114 notice is a severe governance intervention triggered when a council cannot meet its liabilities and halts discretionary expenditure immediately.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is an emergency measure that signals insolvency risk and material uncertainty over a council's ability to continue operations. For a lender, it represents the worst-case financial outcome short of the council entering administration.
findings.figures: 2028/29 financial projection triggers S114 risk if Vesting Day (1 April 2028) is delayed
findings.quote: the MTFS and related risks will be kept under constant review during the year and will be brought to the new council's attention at the earliest opportunity to draw attention to the 2028/29 financial projection, which otherwise will, based upon these projections, require a S114(3) if the council were delayed or not to be absorbed into a new council on 1st April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council's entire savings plan depends on achieving capital receipts from asset sales in specific timescales; any slippage forces immediate emergency expenditure cuts.
findings.detail: The MTFS budget is built on the assumption that planned asset disposals will be completed and credited on time. If these sales slip or fetch lower values, the council has no other mitigation—it must cut spending in-year to balance the budget. The council explicitly warns that 'further slippage in the timing and value of capital receipts during 2026/27' will force compensatory cuts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's budget plan is resilient. When a council cannot balance its books without selling assets on a fixed timeline, that plan is fragile and vulnerable to market conditions or legal delays.
findings.figures: Planned asset receipts are material to reducing borrowing costs and MRP; no specific forward figure given but identified as 'a material element'
findings.quote: Should there be any further slippage in the timing and value of capital receipts during 2026/27, the council will have to compensate by an appropriate level of in year expenditure reductions.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Ongoing structural deficit will continue beyond the council's planned merger date, with £11.94m total shortfall over four years requiring reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The council faces a recurrent annual deficit that continues past the April 2028 Vesting Day when it merges into a new unitary. Even after accounting for planned asset sales reducing the shortfall to £3.962m, the council will draw down £3.05m of reserves between 2026-2028. This leaves an uncertain financial position for the new authority.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves indicate structural spending exceeds revenue, and the deficit persists beyond the restructuring—meaning the new council inherits an unsustainable position unless urgent action is taken.
findings.figures: £11.94m gross deficit 2026/27–2029/30; £3.962m shortfall after asset sales; £3.05m reserve drawdown 2026–2028; £3.384m useable reserves projected at Vesting Day
findings.quote: The proposed 2026/27 MTFS therefore has an ongoing recurrent annual deficit going beyond Vesting Day.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Short-term debt maturity remains elevated at 53% due within 12 months, creating near-term refinancing risk
findings.detail: Although the council has reduced the proportion of loans maturing within 12 months from 91% to 53%, this remains a significant refinancing risk. Half of the £159.0m borrowing portfolio matures within the next 12 months and will need to be refinanced, potentially in a higher interest rate environment or tighter credit conditions.
findings.matters: High short-term maturity concentration creates refinancing risk. If market access tightens or rates rise materially, the council faces higher costs on rollover. The near-term refinancing cliff is a key credit risk metric.
findings.figures: 53% of loans due within 12 months (down from 91% previous year); approximately £80m of £159.0m borrowing due within 12 months
findings.quote: The Council has taken recent steps to reduce the proportion of loans maturing in under 12 months: this is now 53% of loans in contrast to the previous year when this was 91% of loans.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council contingent on imminent local government reorganisation in its treasury strategy; states it has only two years remaining
findings.detail: Paragraph 4.6 of the borrowing strategy states: 'the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account.' This appears to reference a planned local government reorganisation or merger affecting Rushmoor. This creates uncertainty over the appropriateness of treasury forecasts beyond 2027-28 and affects the council's ability to lock in long-term borrowing arrangements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a structural change to the council (merger, reorganisation) is imminent and how this affects the council's financial obligations and treasury management autonomy. This is material to credit assessment and loan agreements.
findings.figures: Two-year timeframe before restructuring
findings.quote: However, the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio shows cumulative losses and council is heavily dependent on investment income to balance budget
findings.detail: The council holds £148.2m in commercial property investments with a cumulative unrealised loss of £11.2m (purchase cost £159.4m vs. value in accounts £148.2m). Significant sector losses include retail (£14.8m) and offices (£7.0m). More significantly, the council relies on investment income to fund 29.5% of gross service expenditure in 2026-27 (forecast investment income £10.1m against gross service expenditure £34.2m). The strategy states that if properties fall below purchase cost at year-end, an updated strategy will be presented to council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's revenue dependency on asset values and market returns. A downturn in property values or rental income would create both balance sheet losses and revenue budget shortfalls. This represents significant concentration risk.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio value £148.2m (purchase cost £159.4m, loss £11.2m); investment income £10.1m forecast 2026-27; gross service expenditure £34.2m; investment income represents 29.5% of service expenditure
findings.quote: The Council has become increasingly dependent on surplus generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Strategic shift to internal borrowing reduces external debt but depletes cash reserves significantly
findings.detail: The council is reducing reliance on external borrowing in favour of internal borrowing (using cash reserves). External borrowing is forecast to fall sharply from £166.0m (2024-25 actual) to £75.0m (2026-27) to £25.0m (2028-29). Simultaneously, internal borrowing is forecast to increase from £7.9m to £110.5m over the same period. This strategy depletes the council's available working capital significantly and increases vulnerability to cash flow disruptions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council is managing its liquidity and whether internal borrowing (depleting reserves) is sustainable. High internal borrowing reduces financial flexibility and cash buffers.
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council planning £70m additional borrowing by 2028-29 despite falling Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to decrease from £174.2m to £135.5m over the forecast period, yet the council expects to need £70.0m of additional borrowing by 2028-29. This is driven by a significant refinancing requirement: £159.0m of loans were held as at 31 December 2025, with around half maturing within 12 months and the remainder within 5 years. The underlying need to refinance maturing debt outweighs the declining CFR.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt maturity profile and refinancing needs. Large refinancing requirements over the next 5 years create refinancing risk, particularly in a rising interest rate environment or credit stress.
findings.figures: £159.0m borrowing at 31 Dec 2025; £70.0m additional borrowing needed by 2028-29; around half of current debt due within 12 months; remaining loans due within 5 years
findings.quote: a significant proportion of the currently held loans are due to mature over the next five years' and will need to be replaced, meaning the Council can expect to have an ongoing borrowing need in future even though the CFR is falling. Over the forecast period above it is expected that £70.0m of additional borrowing will be needed by 2028-29.

findings.paper_title: 9. FIN2607 - Treasury Management Q3
findings.headline: Council releases £1m contingency reserve citing current budgetary pressures
findings.detail: Council had set aside £1m reserve to cover potential accounting impact from statutory override on pooled fund investments. MHCLG extended the override to 2029, removing the original risk. Council has decided to release the reserve 'given current budgetary pressures'. While override extension provides technical justification, the reference to budgetary pressures indicates operational cash pressure prompting reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Reserve release to address cash needs indicates underlying financial pressure, even when the specific reserve is no longer needed for original purpose. Signals council is mobilizing contingency buffers to meet current obligations.
findings.figures: £1m reserve released; pooled fund investments reduced from £16m to £13m
findings.quote: Given current budgetary pressures and the extension of the override the authority decided to release £1m from this reserve.

findings.paper_title: 9. FIN2607 - Treasury Management Q3
findings.headline: S151 officer authorized investment of £10m against £6m treasury strategy limit
findings.detail: In November 2025, S151 officer authorized investment of £10m with a local authority when council's own strategy limit was £6m per counterparty. Council had excess cash holdings in own bank exceeding £3m limit and chose to breach investment limits to achieve favourable rates. Three-month facility maturing 30th January 2026. Justification: zero counterparty risk as all local authorities have PWLB recourse.
findings.matters: Policy limit breach indicates either weak control framework or mismatch between limits and operational cash management needs. S151-level override of treasury strategy suggests policy constraints may not bind against excess liquidity.
findings.figures: £10m invested vs £6m limit (£4m excess); 3-month term; cash holdings exceeded own £3m limit
findings.quote: During quarter 3 the Council exceeded its TM limits for investment in counterparties. The TM strategy limit set on a single local authority and single money market fund is £6m. At the beginning of November the council had a significant cash holding in excess of the cash limit of £3m in our own bank (as per the treasury strategy) with all the councils money market funds accounts fully invested to the £6m limit, the decision was taken by the s151 to invest £10m (i.e. £4m over limit) with a local authority for a short term (3 months) at a favourable rate and the amount is due to be repaid on the 30th January.

findings.paper_title: 9. FIN2607 - Treasury Management Q3
findings.headline: Council holds £148m in commercial property investments and signals need to review exit before additional borrowing
findings.detail: Council directly owns £148m in commercial property, plus £6.5m in business loans and £1.4m in subsidiaries (£155.9m total non-treasury investments). Council explicitly states it must review options for exiting these commercial holdings before undertaking further borrowing, indicating property portfolio is a material constraint on financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Large concentration in single illiquid asset class (commercial property) creates refinancing risk and constrains borrowing capacity. Council's stated requirement to review exit strategies before additional borrowing shows property holdings are treated as a binding financial constraint.
findings.figures: £148m directly owned property; £6.5m loans to businesses; £1.4m subsidiaries; total £155.9m in non-treasury investments
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £148m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: 9. FIN2607 - Treasury Management Q3
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to drop from £12.3m to £3.6m next year
findings.detail: Council's capital budget for 2025/26 is £12.3m but forecast falls sharply to £3.6m in 2026/27 and £2.7m in 2027/28, down from £14.6m actual in 2024/25. Main projects completed to date were Union Yard and Aldershot Crematorium. The pattern suggests either completion of major schemes or financial constraint on new capital investment.
findings.matters: Material reduction in capital investment indicates either project cycle completion or constrained capacity to fund new infrastructure, affecting long-term asset quality and service delivery capacity
findings.quote: The main General Fund capital projects to date have included Union Yard, and Aldershot Crematorium.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Journal entry above £20,000 for PPE impairment lacked required Deputy Section 151 Officer approval and review
findings.detail: During testing of journal authorisation controls, EY found that a journal entry above £20,000 relating to a PPE impairment was not properly reviewed and authorised by the Deputy Section 151 Officer as required by management policy. While EY determined the underlying adjustment was supportable, the control failure represents a material gap in financial review procedures.
findings.matters: Weak journal authorisation controls are a primary fraud risk and allow errors or irregularities to be processed without oversight. This is a fundamental control that underpins financial reporting accuracy.
findings.figures: Journal above £20,000 threshold without proper evidence of review
findings.quote: During journal testing, we were unable to obtained evidence that a journal above £20,000 was approved by Deputy S151 officer as required in terms of management policy on processing journals.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Rising borrowing costs present a material risk to the council's financial sustainability.
findings.detail: EY identified as a value-for-money risk that the current level of external debt and the impact of increased borrowing costs pose a significant risk to the Council's financial sustainability. The council has replaced short-term with long-term borrowing to reduce interest rate volatility, but the underlying scale of debt servicing costs remains a material concern.
findings.matters: Higher debt servicing costs consume growing portions of the budget, reducing flexibility to respond to demand shocks, service changes, or other financial pressures. Combined with reserve depletion, this creates a structural funding crisis.
findings.figures: £40 million asset disposal programme undertaken to achieve interest and cost reduction savings
findings.quote: Risk 1 – Level of external borrowing - The current level of debt and the impact of increased borrowing costs presents a risk to the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Council's Stability and Resilience Reserve will be fully depleted by 2027/28 if savings targets are not met.
findings.detail: EY identified a VFM risk of significant weakness: the Council is using its Stability and Resilience Reserve to balance the budget in the short term, and the reserve will be drawn down entirely over the MTFS period if projected savings do not materialise. This would leave the Council with insufficient reserves to set a balanced budget or absorb any further deficit in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion within 2-3 years creates immediate liquidity crisis risk. Without adequate reserves, the council cannot manage spending volatility or implement emergency measures, forcing service cuts or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Reserves projected to be exhausted by 2027/28 if current trajectory continues
findings.quote: The Stability and Resilience Reserve is being used to balance the budget in the short-term and will be depleted over the MTFS period, if no savings materialise. Therefore, the Council will have insufficient reserves in 2027/28 to set a balanced budget or cover further projected deficit.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion anticipated for 2024/25 because sufficient evidence cannot be obtained over financial statement balances.
findings.detail: EY anticipates issuing a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. Although the level of assurance gained has increased, the auditor has not obtained sufficient evidence over all in-year movements and closing balances. Because the 2023/24 audit was also disclaimed, there is no assurance over brought-forward balances from that year. The auditor is unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means no reliance can be placed on the council's published financial statements. This is a fundamental red flag for lenders and signals severe weaknesses in financial reporting and internal control.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions issued on 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23; 2024/25 anticipated to be disclaimed
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Item 9. Treasury Management Q2 Report
findings.headline: Strategic pooled fund closure required loss mitigation during the period
findings.detail: One of the council's strategic pooled funds closed during the first half of 2025/26. The council had to sell investments from other funds to 'mitigate the losses' of the closing fund. Strategic pooled funds fell from £16m to £13m as a result.
findings.matters: Fund closure and required loss realisation indicate underperformance and volatility in the council's commercial investment portfolio. This directly reduces the income returns the council relies on and signals deterioration in asset quality.
findings.figures: Strategic pooled funds reduced from £16m to £13m; one fund closed
findings.quote: the sale of some funds to mitigate the losses of a fund which was closing

findings.paper_title: Item 9. Treasury Management Q2 Report
findings.headline: 56% of net revenue stream depends on volatile commercial investment returns
findings.detail: Service and commercial investments generated £7.9m income on a net revenue stream of approximately £14m (56.54% of total). This proportion is far above prudent levels for councils, creating severe exposure to market downturns and investment performance volatility.
findings.matters: Lenders assess revenue sustainability as a core measure of council solvency. Dependence on market-driven investment returns for over half of annual revenue creates exposure to budget deficits during market downturns and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £7.9m income from commercial/service investments; 56.54% of net revenue stream
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream 56.54%

findings.paper_title: Item 9. Treasury Management Q2 Report
findings.headline: Investment income running £85k behind budget at midyear
findings.detail: The council budgeted £540k income from strategic pooled funds in 2025/26. By end of September (halfway through the year), only £455k was received. This shortfall is material given the council's dependence on commercial investment returns.
findings.matters: Commercial investment income represents 56% of the council's net revenue stream. Underperformance against budget at midyear indicates either market volatility or asset value declines, and threatens the reliability of the planned income the budget depends on.
findings.figures: £540k budgeted; £455k received by 30 Sept; £85k shortfall at midpoint
findings.quote: The Authority has budgeted £540k income from these investments in 2025/26. Income received up to 30th September was £455k.

findings.paper_title: Item 9. Treasury Management Q2 Report
findings.headline: Council released £1m prudent reserve due to budget pressures
findings.detail: The council had set aside £1m to protect against accounting impacts from pooled investment fund volatility. With the statutory override extended by MHCLG, they released the reserve. Notably, the decision is justified by 'current budgetary pressures', signalling financial tightness.
findings.matters: Releasing prudent reserves due to budget pressures indicates financial strain and reduced resilience. It suggests the budget position is tighter than routine compliance reporting shows, limiting the council's ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: £1m reserve released
findings.quote: The Authority had set up a reserve of £1m to mitigate the impact of the statutory override not being extended. Given current budgetary pressures and the extension of the override the authority decided to release £1m from this reserve.

findings.paper_title: Item 9. Treasury Management Q2 Report
findings.headline: £148m commercial property portfolio constrains future borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The council holds £148m in commercial investments purchased before CIPFA Prudential Code changes that now restrict borrowing for similar purposes. The council explicitly states it will 'review options for exiting these investments' before taking further borrowing, creating a material constraint on capital funding flexibility.
findings.matters: This is a structural constraint on the council's ability to fund capital programmes. Any new borrowing for capital projects requires first exiting a £148m portfolio, which delays investment and forces realisation of losses if asset prices are unfavourable.
findings.figures: £148m directly owned property; £6.5m loans to businesses; £1.4m subsidiaries; total non-treasury investments £155.9m
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £148m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments.

news_drafts.headline: Rushmoor's auditor expects to issue a qualified opinion on the council's 2025/26 accounts
news_drafts.lead:
Rushmoor Borough Council's external auditor expects to issue a qualified opinion on its 2025/26 accounts, which means it could not fully sign them off. The auditor's draft audit results report, put to the Audit and Governance Committee, says the audit is substantially complete and that, subject to outstanding procedures and review, "we expect to issue a qualified opinion."

The report says an unqualified opinion may be possible by 2027/28, on the audit recovery trajectory set by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

The council's annual risk management update records the risk that an unqualified opinion is delayed at a residual score of 6, rated Medium. The register says the return to an unqualified opinion by 2027/28 has been delayed by lack of progress on valuations of property, plant and equipment, on reserves and on disclosures. Mitigations listed are new valuers procured and an improved working relationship with its external auditors, EY. The register's entry reads: "Improved position on 25/26 accounts, back on track for fully qualified accounts. Continuing to work with auditors."

news_drafts.headline: Hampshire County Council considers seeking exceptional financial support for its 2027/28 budget
news_drafts.lead:
Hampshire County Council is considering a request for exceptional financial support to help balance its budget for 2027/28, according to its budget consultation information pack for that year. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or use capital resources, to cover day-to-day spending. It is a last resort for councils.

The pack says the support would allow borrowing or capital resources to fund day-to-day costs. It says the support would become a future liability, repaid over 20 years, and would not close the underlying gap in the budget.

The pack also gives the number of councils that have received the support. It says government granted it to "36 councils in the 2026/27 financial year". Of those 36, 33 (92%) are authorities responsible for social care and for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

news_drafts.headline: Rushmoor reports £1.2m saved on interest and debt repayment, mostly from two property sales and an early loan repayment
news_drafts.lead:
Rushmoor Borough Council has saved £1.2m on the cost of its borrowing this year, according to the month 4 budget report before its Cabinet on 20 October. Interest costs are £758k lower than budgeted. The council has also set aside £427k less than budgeted for its minimum revenue provision (MRP), the amount a council must put aside from each year's budget to pay off past borrowing, much like a mortgage repayment.

The report says the savings come largely from the sale of two properties, 168 High Street for £2m and Optrex Lane for £1.5m. They also come from the early repayment of a £2.1m loan by Farnborough International.

The savings form part of the council's budget monitoring, its in-year check of spending against budget, and they contribute to the headline underspend. The report describes them as one-off items that do not reflect a structural improvement in the budget.
